title: View vs conflict serializability

transcript.text: Two transactions run at the same time. When is their interleaving still correct? The course gives two answers: view-serializability and conflict-serializability. They are not the same thing, and the difference is a classic exam trap.

A schedule is serializable if it leaves the database in the same state as some serial schedule of the same transactions. To check that, we need a notion of equivalence, and each notion gives a different class of schedules.

View-equivalence asks for three things: the same operations, every read reads from the same write, and every object gets its final value from the same write. A schedule that is view-equivalent to a serial one is in VSR.
Conflict-serializability is stricter. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, touch the same object, and at least one of them is a write. Two reads never conflict.
Take this schedule from the slides. T1 reads x, T2 writes x, T1 writes x, and T3 writes x. T2 and T1 write x without reading it first: these are blind writes.

Now build the conflict graph: one node per transaction, one arc for every conflicting pair, in order. r1 before w2 gives an arc from T1 to T2, and w2 before w1 gives an arc from T2 back to T1. That is a cycle, so the schedule is not conflict-serializable.

Yet compare it with the serial schedule T1, T2, T3. T1 still reads the initial value of x, and T3 still writes the final value. Same reads-from, same final write: the schedule is view-serializable. The blind writes in the middle are overwritten, so their order does not matter to anyone.

So every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable, but not the other way around. A cycle in the conflict graph rules out CSR, not VSR. Deciding VSR is much harder, which is why real schedulers rely on the conflict test.

notes_md:
## Key ideas
- **Serializable schedule**: leaves the database in the same state as some serial schedule of the same transactions [02-Concurrency.pdf p.20].
- **View-equivalence**: same operations, same *reads-from* relation, same *final writes*. VSR = schedules view-equivalent to a serial one [02-Concurrency.pdf p.22].
- **Conflict**: two operations of different transactions on the same object, at least one a write (r-w, w-r, w-w). Two reads never conflict [02-Concurrency.pdf p.32].
- **Conflict graph**: one node per transaction, an arc Ti → Tj when an operation of Ti conflicts with and precedes one of Tj. S ∈ CSR ⇔ the graph is acyclic [02-Concurrency.pdf p.37].
- **CSR ⊂ VSR**: every CSR schedule is VSR, not the converse [02-Concurrency.pdf p.34].

## Worked example
`r1(x) w2(x) w1(x) w3(x)` has the cycle T1 → T2 → T1, so it is **not CSR**. It is still **VSR**: it is view-equivalent to the serial T1 T2 T3, because the blind writes w2(x), w1(x) are overwritten by w3(x) [02-Concurrency.pdf p.41].

## Watch out
- A cycle in the conflict graph rules out CSR, **not** VSR.
- Deciding VSR is computationally hard; schedulers use conflict-based tests [02-Concurrency.pdf p.30].

quiz.question: The conflict graph of a schedule S contains a cycle. What can you conclude?
options: S is neither CSR nor VSR
S is not CSR, but it may still be VSR
S is VSR but not serial
quiz.explanation: An acyclic conflict graph is equivalent to CSR, so a cycle rules out CSR. VSR is a larger class: r1(x) w2(x) w1(x) w3(x) has a cycle and is still VSR.
